articles.title: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
articles.summary: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors. “I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.
body: It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.
But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.

One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.
Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.
points: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors.

articles.title: Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline
articles.summary: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators. It started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn.
body: I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes.

It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t.

It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing as Caroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it.

Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicine contacted me to ask whether I’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well.
points: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators.

articles.title: ‘It feels like the light is pushing the darkness apart’: Gellért Gombai’s best phone picture
articles.summary: The photographer was holidaying with his family when two shadows became a plaything for his young son. Gellért Gombai, his wife and two children spend much of the year at their home in Budapest, Hungary, but most of their summers in Alsóörs.
body: On this particular day, the family had eaten hotdogs for lunch, before Gombai had taken the kids, Lóci and Janka, to the playground. “Lóci, who was five at the time, was jumping between two shadows – one from a changing room, and the other from a building’s roof,” he says. “I asked him to stay still for a few minutes while I got the shot, and he lay like this on the ground. He’s a big-hearted little clown; I’m so glad he’s my son.” When he showed the children, “Janka immediately asked me to take the same shot of her, which often happens. Lóci said it looked like he was among mountains, or as though a monster was about to eat him.”

Gombai applied his phone’s “dramatic cool” filter, and made some minor adjustments. “I really liked the slightly metaphysical spaces created by light and shadow,” he says. “If I forget for a moment it’s my son, I see a carefree form lying in the light while the darkness has bitten a large piece out of the space. Even still, it doesn’t feel sad to me. I have the feeling that the light is pushing the darkness apart.”

articles.title: Alexandra Shulman: ‘Which book am I ashamed not to have read? Literally the whole canon of classic English literature’
articles.summary: The former British Vogue editor-in-chief and author on a romantic kiss on a traffic island, her school-run regrets, and a very expensive nude. Born in London, Alexandra Shulman, 68, studied social anthropology at the University of Sussex.
body: When were you happiest? Anytime that I’m lying in the sun next to a swimming pool with a good book.
Which living person do you most admire, and why? The king, for the amount of work he’s doing while going through cancer treatment.
Aside from property, what’s the most expensive thing you’ve bought? A Roger Hilton gouache of a nude.
What would your superpower be? To teleport myself to places so I didn’t have to go on a plane.

articles.title: Homemade McGriddles
articles.summary: The key part of any good copycat recipe is that one hard-to-pinpoint flavor component that makes the whole thing light up the nostalgia part of your brain. Without it, even a delicious meal feels a little bit like a letdown.
body: Make homemade breakfast sandwiches better than the fast-food classic using instant pancake (or biscuit) mix with fluffy maple-glazed pancakes, eggs, American cheese, and crispy bacon.

Because we’re going to the trouble of making this at home, there have to be a few upgrades. Greek yogurt in the batter adds a boost of tang and protein and keeps the pancakes firm enough while cooking to keep their shape. A fluffy folded egg bakes alongside thick-cut bacon in the oven. But, perhaps most importantly, use the nicest maple syrup you can find. It’s a good thing they reheat well, so I can enjoy my nostalgic little breakfast treat throughout the week.

Arrange two racks to divide the oven into thirds. Heat the oven to 350ºF. Meanwhile, arrange 6 halved thick-cut bacon slices in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Place on the lower rack while the oven is heating up and bake until crisp, 25 to 40 minutes total. Meanwhile, make the pancakes and eggs.
points: The key part of any good copycat recipe is that one hard-to-pinpoint flavor component that makes the whole thing light up the nostalgia part of your brain.

articles.title: My Favorite Airbnb: A Hudson Valley Retreat With a Creekside Hot Tub and Sauna
articles.summary: Between its storybook interiors and proximity to small-town shops, farm stands, & cider orchards, this Hudson Valley stay is one of my top upstate discoveries.
body: Getting 12 people to agree on a weekend away is an exercise in logistics. Someone wants to hike; someone else would rather browse antique shops; a few people are already asking what’s for dinner. My ideal group getaway? One that leaves room for all of it, with a house you're excited to return to in between excursions. On a recent October weekend, my friends and I—a total of six couples—found that combination at Schoonmaker Retreat, tucked in the quaint Hudson Valley hamlet of High Falls.

As a lifelong New Yorker, I’ve made plenty of trips to the Catskills and Hudson Valley, but High Falls, Rosendale, and Accord were towns I hadn’t yet gotten to know. Rosendale had been on my radar thanks to the introduction of Six Bells Countryside Inn, a delightfully whimsical, British-inspired hotel, and the surrounding area seemed ripe for a fall weekend of vintage shopping, cider tasting, and lots of leaf-peeping. We lucked into a real Goldilocks window, with timing just right for trees to stand ablaze with reds, yellows, and the last bits of green. The weather was crisp, but still sunny enough to sit outside for hours, from long orchard lunches to cozy s’more nights.
points: Between its storybook interiors and proximity to small-town shops, farm stands, & cider orchards, this Hudson Valley stay is one of my top upstate discoveries.

articles.title: The 25 Best Airbnbs in Italy, From Puglia to the Dolomites
articles.summary: Whether you’re dreaming of rugged coastlines or rambling hillsides, these are the best Airbnbs to book in Italy, from Puglia to Tuscany to the Amalfi Coast.
body: There is always a reason to talk about Italy. Perhaps it’s to celebrate the country’s craft heritage, which has been passed down for generations. Or to explore the merits of its multitudinous pasta shapes and grape varietals (around 500 each, if you can believe). The natural landscapes are so mind-bogglingly beautiful they tend to invite clichés, and the country’s landmarks—from Rome’s Colosseum to Florence’s Ponte Vecchio—manage to awe and inspire even the most jaded travelers among us. Suffice it to say, it is always a good time to visit Italy.

If you’re itching to plan a dolce vita getaway, start by perusing the compelling vacation rentals below to pick out a home base. We’ve scoured listings in the country’s most breathtaking regions—from a Sardinian home with a sea access staircase built into the rocks, to a 1700s-era apartment nestled in the old Sicilian town of Modica. Or perhaps you’re in need of isolation? We found a home in a car-free, medieval village in the hills of Tuscany. Whatever your pursuit, the 25 Airbnbs below deliver in spades.

articles.title: Chili con Carne
body: A Texan classic that utilizes ground beef to speed things up, but keeps all the flavors of the original, like ancho, poblano, and jalapeno chiles.

Chili con carne can take many forms depending on what family the recipe originates from, but it’s typically a spicy, hearty stew made with chili powder, meat (usually beef), tomatoes, and sometimes beans. For this version, we’re taking a distinctly Texan approach: a no-bean chili that puts the focus on the beef, chiles, and spices.

Traditional Texas chili is made by stewing chunks of beef chuck in a tomato-based sauce made with whole dried chiles. This chili con carne is a fast track to those flavors, utilizing quicker-cooking ground beef and ancho chile powder. You can substitute regular chili powder, but I prefer ancho chile here because it delivers a purer chile flavor that’s closer to that of whole dried chiles. Chili powder often contains a blend of other spices and sometimes salt. Making your own spice mix achieves the right balance in every pot.
points: A Texan classic that utilizes ground beef to speed things up, but keeps all the flavors of the original, like ancho, poblano, and jalapeno chiles.

articles.title: The “Cowboy Candy” Seasoning Blend That Makes Chicken Thighs Taste Ridiculously Amazing
articles.summary: It’s amazing on potatoes, too! READ MORE...
body: One of my favorite dinners to make is juicy chicken thighs. Pan-seared or oven-roasted, they’re delicious with a range of different seasonings and marinades. Recently, Spiceology dropped a new seasoning blend based on a sweet and spicy Texan condiment that is absolutely spectacular on chicken thighs (among other dishes). It’s so good, I have not stopped telling everyone about it!

Spiceology has all sorts of delicious spices and seasoning blends including Nashville Hot Chicken Seasoning, Greek Freak Mediterranean Seasoning, and Derek Wolf Cowboy Butter, which is an editor-favorite that came out last fall. Derek Wolf, an expert of cooking over fire, teamed up with Spiceology once again to launch the new Cowboy Candy Seasoning in late July.

A staple started in 1920s Texas, cowboy candy itself is basically candied jalapeños ( we have a great recipe!). This seasoning turns the sweet, spicy, vinegar-y flavors of the Texan topping into a dry blend you can sprinkle onto veggies, chicken, steak, seafood, or even mix into butter and spread on top of Southern cornbread.
